Lessons.Title: Sort Quadrilaterals
ExplanationParagraphs: Original Grade5 U07:L04 asks pupils to SORT quadrilaterals using sides, angle sizes and the number of parallel or perpendicular pairs, then recognize possible inclusion relationships from the actual physical shapes.

Warm-up What Do You Know About Quadrilaterals? is an OPEN elicitation. A four-sided polygon can have zero, one or two parallel opposite-side pairs, and a square has four equal edges and four right angles.

Activity1 Guess Which One: partner secretly selects one of the original eight diagram quadrilaterals; the other uses YES/NO geometry attribute questions, crosses out impossible cards and defends elimination. Actual source figure drawings are teacher assessed; the final two Han/Mai figure images are not certified numerically.

Activity2 Quadrilateral Card Sort gives publisher cards, asks each student to sort once and then AGAIN with different named criteria. Parallel side counts, equal side lengths and right angles are defensible groupings, but there is no unique prescribed sequence and the source card deck is teacher-reviewed.

Existing correct Rich V2 examples of coordinate quadrilaterals remain optional extensions. Exact selected Practice checks only classroom vocabulary and bounded attributes; two independent sorts and source drawings are teacher-scored.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Goal: describe and SORT quadrilaterals using precise attributes of sides and angles, including parallel and perpendicular pairs, with more than one defensible sorting rule. The 2021 source begins with a partner-only Guess Which One game and then invites two different card sorts before specifying a sort based on parallel lines.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Warm-up — ask useful questions: student A secretly selects one figure from an original first-party set containing a square, a slanted rhombus, a non-rectangle parallelogram, and an irregular quadrilateral. Student B asks yes/no questions such as 'Does it have two pairs of parallel sides?' or 'Does it have four right angles?', and narrows the possibilities. Teacher checks that the question actually applies to visible attributes and that the chosen figure can be identified.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 1 — two independent categories: first sort original shapes by two pairs/one pair/no pairs of parallel opposite sides, then sort by number of right angles or equal side lengths. For example, a square and non-square rhombus each have four equal sides, but only the square is a rectangle. A typical parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides without four right angles.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 2 — reason across categories: prove that a square is a rectangle and rhombus, but an irregular quadrilateral may be neither. Describe one figure by four vertices (0,0),(4,0),(3,2),(0,2) and use coordinates to check its top and bottom sides are parallel while other opposite sides are not. In the 2021 inclusive trapezoid convention, it is a trapezoid. The learner must draw the original shape and defend each claim.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Assessment: the actual game, physical/source card images, category sorting, partner critique and figure drawings are teacher-reviewed. A simple 'square' multiple-choice answer cannot certify classification reasoning or actual visual access.

KeyConcepts.Title: Quadrilateral classification
KeyConcepts.Definition: A quadrilateral is a four-straight-sided closed polygon; defining side and angle attributes determine more specific classes.
KeyConcepts.Rule: A square has two parallel opposite side pairs, four equal sides, and four right angles.
KeyConcepts.Example: It belongs to rectangle and rhombus classes.

KeyConcepts.Title: Parallel pairs
KeyConcepts.Definition: Opposite straight sides remain equidistant when extended and do not intersect.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Parallelograms have two parallel opposite side pairs.
KeyConcepts.Example: An irregular quadrilateral need not have parallel sides.

KeyConcepts.Title: Multiple sorting systems
KeyConcepts.Definition: A collection may be validly grouped in distinct ways.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Side-length equality and right-angle count give distinct classification criteria.
KeyConcepts.Example: A non-square rhombus fits all-equal sides but not all-right angles.

Lessons.Title: Trapezoids PLC Activity
ExplanationParagraphs: Original 2021 Grade5 U07:L05 explicitly compares two common definitions of trapezoid. Exclusive definition means EXACTLY one pair of parallel opposite sides; inclusive definition means AT LEAST one. The curriculum deliberately adopts the INCLUSIVE definition in Activity2.

Warm-up What Do You Know About Trapezoids? collects student prior definitions before the class adopts a convention; classify without declaring one definition globally correct for every mathematical context.

Activity1 What’s a Trapezoid? asks pupils to DRAW a trapezoid on coordinate grid, label vertices and decide whether it is also square, rectangle, rhombus or parallelogram. Multiple drawings are possible; selected choices cannot certify their actual sketches.

Activity2 Two Definitions gives exact printed Definition1/Definition2 and FIVE statements about all/no/some parallelograms and trapezoids. Under inclusive course rule every parallelogram and square qualifies; not every trapezoid is a parallelogram. Under exclusive no parallelogram qualifies.

Prior example coordinate constructions in Rich V2 are independent support. Teacher reviews source drawings, justifications and classification of images; bounded selected Practice checks definition logic only.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Goal: compare TWO mathematically used trapezoid definitions: exclusive 'exactly one pair of parallel opposite sides' and inclusive 'at least one pair'. The 2021 lesson explicitly adopts the INCLUSIVE definition as its course convention; classification under each rule must not be silently treated as interchangeable.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Warm-up: draw a sloping four-sided figure with one pair of horizontal opposite sides and no other parallel pair. Name its visible parallel lines and explain why it satisfies both definitions, no matter whether it is drawn upright or rotated.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 1 — coordinate construction: draw vertices (0,0),(5,0),(4,2),(1,2), which form a trapezoid with a parallel horizontal base and top but the two other sides have different slopes. Draw a separate parallelogram with vertices (0,0),(4,0),(5,2),(1,2), whose two opposite side pairs are both parallel. Classify both figures under the exactly-one versus at-least-one definition. Require labeled coordinate diagrams and explanations of line directions.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 2 — hierarchy comparison: with the inclusive convention, every parallelogram is a trapezoid but not every trapezoid is a parallelogram. With the exclusive convention, no parallelogram is a trapezoid. A square is a trapezoid ONLY under the inclusive convention, and every square is also a parallelogram; the learner evaluates this statement and creates a visual hierarchy consistent with the selected definition.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Assessment: a numeric or category label alone cannot establish coordinate drawing correctness or understanding of why the two definitions create different hierarchy diagrams. Teacher reviews the actual shapes, diagrams and discussion; the source's copyrighted illustrations and response cards were not reused.

KeyConcepts.Title: Exclusive trapezoid definition
KeyConcepts.Definition: Some sources reserve trapezoid for quadrilaterals with exactly one parallel opposite side pair.
KeyConcepts.Rule: A parallelogram is not a trapezoid under the exclusive rule.
KeyConcepts.Example: A non-parallelogram with exactly one parallel pair meets it.

KeyConcepts.Title: Inclusive trapezoid definition used in 2021 lesson
KeyConcepts.Definition: The Edulytiks mapping to this source must adopt a quadrilateral with at least one parallel opposite side pair.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Every parallelogram is a trapezoid in the inclusive hierarchy.
KeyConcepts.Example: A square is also a trapezoid by this rule.

KeyConcepts.Title: Classification depends on definitions
KeyConcepts.Definition: Different classroom conventions produce different relationships without changing a shape's geometric properties.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Under inclusive: parallelograms ⊂ trapezoids; exclusive: disjoint.
KeyConcepts.Example: Always label the convention in solutions and rubrics.

Lessons.Title: Hierarchy of Quadrilaterals
ExplanationParagraphs: Original 2021 Grade5 U07:L06 organizes quadrilateral SUBCATEGORIES via the defining properties of side lengths, parallel sides and right angles, retaining the curriculum's inclusive trapezoid definition.
Warm-up Notice and Wonder Squares and Rhombuses compares source shapes by equal sides and angle measures, showing the difference between being a rhombus and the more specific square.

Activity1 Shapes with Toothpicks: with FOUR equal toothpicks build a square then a slanted rhombus while all edge lengths remain fixed but angles change; using SIX sticks with opposite-side lengths build a rectangle and a nonrectangular parallelogram. Learners construct and explain.

Activity2 Three Quadrilaterals asks pupils to draw three distinct polygons (at least one parallelogram), evaluate square/rhombus/rectangle/parallelogram and additionally DRAW a rhombus not square plus one that is square. Diego argues there cannot be a square not a rhombus: correct under source properties.

Automated selected Practice covers bounded subset truths but cannot verify toothpick constructions, original source pictures or learner-created coordinates. Existing Rich V2 content reused; teacher drawings and explanations are recorded as mandatory review.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Goal: construct quadrilaterals physically from identical straight sticks and explain inclusion relationships: every square is a rhombus; every rectangle is a parallelogram, but converses need not hold. The source uses four or six toothpicks to demonstrate fixed side lengths while changing angles and then asks students to critique a misleading explanation.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Warm-up: take four hypothetical equal toothpicks and connect their endpoints as a square. Rotate/joint the shape into a slanted, non-right-angled rhombus without changing the four side lengths. What changed is angle measure, not side length or closed four-sided status.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 1 — two constructions: model a square and a non-square rhombus using four equal sticks. Both have all equal sides; only the square has four right angles. Model a rectangle and a slanted parallelogram with pairs of matching opposite side lengths (for example two short and two long sticks). In both shapes, opposite sides stay parallel but only the rectangle has right angles.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 2 — classify hand-drawn shapes: draw a rhombus with vertices (0,2),(2,3),(4,2),(2,1), which has all four equal side lengths but does NOT have four right angles; draw the axis-aligned square (0,0),(2,0),(2,2),(0,2), which is both square and rhombus. Explain why a 'square that is not a rhombus' is impossible; rewrite the incorrect statement 'Rhombuses are not squares' as 'Some rhombuses are squares; some are not.'

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Assessment: drawing and physical construction, side-length verification, the full hierarchy and partner critique cannot be certified by a single classification label; source activity requires teacher evaluation of actual shapes. First-party coordinate examples replace source toothpick photographs.

KeyConcepts.Title: Rhombus contains squares
KeyConcepts.Definition: A rhombus has four equal sides; a square additionally has four right angles.
KeyConcepts.Example: A slanted rhombus is a counterexample to the converse.

KeyConcepts.Title: Parallelogram contains rectangles
KeyConcepts.Definition: A parallelogram has both opposite side pairs parallel; a rectangle additionally has four right angles.
KeyConcepts.Example: Slanted parallelogram is not a rectangle.

KeyConcepts.Title: Inherited defining properties
KeyConcepts.Definition: Every subclass inherits the required defining properties of its containing class.
KeyConcepts.Rule: A square is simultaneously a rectangle, a rhombus and a parallelogram.
KeyConcepts.Example: No square can fail the four-equal-sides test.

Lessons.Title: Rectangles and Squares
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: reason using always/sometimes/never about shape class hierarchy, recognize which requested quadrilateral combinations are IMPOSSIBLE and give both true examples and counterexamples for 'sometimes'. The source is an attribute-based card game with a gallery walk, not just diagram identification.

Warm-up: consider a square and a rectangle with different adjacent lengths. Both have right angles, yet only the first necessarily has four equal sides. Ask whether every rectangle must be a square and why a long rectangle is a counterexample.

Activity 1 — original clue pairs: choose or draw one quadrilateral that is not a parallelogram, a rhombus that is square, a rhombus that is not square, a rectangle that is not square, and a parallelogram that is not a rectangle. Explain why a 'square that is not a rectangle' cannot exist. Under the inclusive source convention, a rectangle is also a trapezoid; a figure that is a trapezoid and NOT parallelogram can have just one parallel pair.

Activity 2 — classify statements: 'Rhombus is a square': SOMETIMES (right angles required); 'Square is a rhombus': ALWAYS; 'Triangle is quadrilateral': NEVER; 'Square is a rectangle': ALWAYS; 'Rectangle is parallelogram': ALWAYS; 'Parallelogram is rhombus': SOMETIMES. Under the source inclusive trapezoid definition, 'Trapezoid is parallelogram': SOMETIMES. For every SOMETIMES answer supply two diagrams, one supporting example and one counterexample.

Assessment: card use-once constraint, physically meaningful drawings, correct hierarchy definitions and counterexample justifications are teacher-judged; numerical property tests cannot auto-pass the source art/communication task.

KeyConcepts.Title: Always means class inclusion
KeyConcepts.Definition: If every figure in class A satisfies B's definition, 'A is B' is always true.

KeyConcepts.Title: Sometimes requires both evidence types
KeyConcepts.Definition: A sometimes claim needs an example where it holds and another where it fails.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Some rhombuses are squares; a non-right rhombus is not.

KeyConcepts.Title: Never means definitions are incompatible
KeyConcepts.Definition: A triangle has three sides and cannot be a quadrilateral with four sides.
KeyConcepts.Rule: A square cannot fail to be a rectangle.
KeyConcepts.Example: Do not invent impossible geometry for a requested counterexample.

WorkedExamples.Title: Classify rhombus-square relation
WorkedExamples.Question: Is a rhombus always/sometimes/never a square?
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party shape-attribute or counterexample analysis. Student-drawn figures require teacher assessment.
Steps: A rhombus has four equal sides.
A square has four equal sides and four right angles.
Give a square and a non-right rhombus.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both example and counterexample required.

WorkedExamples.Title: Classify square-rectangle relation
WorkedExamples.Question: Is a square always/sometimes/never a rectangle?
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party shape-attribute or counterexample analysis. Student-drawn figures require teacher assessment.
Steps: Read rectangle's four-right-angle requirement.
A square has four right angles.
Conclude all squares qualify.
WorkedExamples.Check: Impossible to draw a square that is not a rectangle.

WorkedExamples.Title: Classify inclusive trapezoids
WorkedExamples.Question: Is a trapezoid always/sometimes/never a parallelogram under the 2021 rule?
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party shape-attribute or counterexample analysis. Student-drawn figures require teacher assessment.
Steps: An inclusive trapezoid has at least one parallel pair.
A parallelogram has two such pairs.
Give a parallelogram and a one-pair trapezoid.
WorkedExamples.Check: Source inclusive convention must be used.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Call trapezoid never parallelogram because of an exclusive definition
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: This lesson uses the inclusive at-least-one convention taught in L05.
CommonMistakes.Correction: A parallelogram meets the inclusive trapezoid definition.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Sometimes requires existence of both a qualifying and nonqualifying instance.

SummaryPoints: Always/sometimes/never statements express inclusion and counterexamples.
No square can fail to be a rectangle or a rhombus.
Teacher reviews actual drawings and card-use rules.

Lessons.Title: Sort Triangles
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: SORT triangles by both side-length relationships and angle type in a 3×3 attribute grid, identify combinations that CANNOT exist, and use all/some/none statements about right triangles. The 2021 source explicitly notes an equilateral triangle cannot be a right or obtuse triangle.

Warm-up: draw an equilateral triangle with three congruent sides and three 60° angles. Compare it with a right triangle having one 90° angle and two acute angles, and with an obtuse triangle having one angle greater than90°. Explain why a triangle can never have two right angles or two obtuse angles because the angle sum is180°.

Activity 1 — fill an original table: columns scalene (three unequal sides), isosceles non-equilateral (exactly two equal sides), equilateral (three equal sides); rows acute, right, obtuse. An equilateral triangle can fill ONLY the acute row. Both scalene and exactly-two-equal-side triangles can be acute or obtuse or right (e.g., right isosceles angles45°,45°,90°). Ask students to draw at least one sample for each allowed cell and explain the empty equilateral-right and equilateral-obtuse cells.

Activity 2 — write quantifiers: ALL right triangles have one right angle and their other two angles acute. SOME right triangles have two equal sides (45°-45°-90°), but not all. NONE have an obtuse angle or all three equal sides. Partner checks whether the learner's drawings and categorical statements satisfy these properties.

Assessment: source card-sort, measured side relations, actual angle/drawing classification, two impossible classes and all/some/none statements require teacher-reviewed figures. The text table is an accessible description but not verified visual parity with publisher figure cards.

KeyConcepts.Title: Triangle side families
KeyConcepts.Definition: Scalene has three distinct side lengths; isosceles non-equilateral exactly two equal sides; equilateral all three equal.

KeyConcepts.Title: Triangle angle types
KeyConcepts.Definition: Acute: three angles <90°; right: one angle90°; obtuse: one angle>90°.
KeyConcepts.Example: A triangle cannot have two right or two obtuse angles.

KeyConcepts.Title: Impossible equilateral pairs
KeyConcepts.Definition: Three equal sides force three equal60° angles, so equilateral is always acute.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Equilateral-right and equilateral-obtuse cells are empty.
KeyConcepts.Example: Give geometric reason, not only no matching card.

WorkedExamples.Title: Classify equilateral triangle
WorkedExamples.Question: Could three equal sides form a right triangle?
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party shape-attribute or counterexample analysis. Student-drawn figures require teacher assessment.
Steps: Equal sides imply equal angles.
Three equal angles summing to180° each are60°.
No angle can be90°.
WorkedExamples.Check: Any equilateral is acute.

WorkedExamples.Title: Describe a right isosceles triangle
WorkedExamples.Question: Can a right triangle have exactly two equal sides?
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party shape-attribute or counterexample analysis. Student-drawn figures require teacher assessment.
Steps: Choose equal perpendicular legs.
Each smaller angle is45° when other right angle is90°.
Check angle total.
WorkedExamples.Check: It has exactly two equal sides, not three.

WorkedExamples.Title: Right triangle quantifiers
WorkedExamples.Question: Write one ALL, SOME and NONE statement about right triangles.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party shape-attribute or counterexample analysis. Student-drawn figures require teacher assessment.
Steps: All have exactly one right angle.
Some have two equal sides.
None has an obtuse angle or three equal sides.
WorkedExamples.Answer: These statements hold under ordinary nondegenerate triangle definitions.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher reviews counterexamples and original drawings.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat every isosceles as having exactly two equal sides without defining category
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Some mathematical conventions include equilateral among isosceles; the grid's source category explicitly says 'exactly two' for one column.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Distinguish exactly two equal from all three equal before sorting.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assume three equal sides could create right or obtuse angles
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use angle sum and equal-angle property.

SummaryPoints: Triangles can be sorted by sides and angle classes simultaneously.
The equilateral-right and equilateral-obtuse cells are impossible.
Source card sorting and all/some/none explanations are teacher-reviewed.
